Yes, when you declare an object of type `std::string` in C++ using the syntax:

```cpp
std::string myString;
```

the default constructor of the `std::string` class is called. In C++11 and later standards, the default constructor of `std::string` creates an empty string. Therefore, `myString` is initialized to be an empty string ("").

In more detailed terms, this constructor initializes the string with a length of zero. Under the hood, implementations typically hold this empty state with no allocated memory or with a small internal buffer ready for use, depending on the implementation details of the standard library used.

C++ standard library (specifically the container classes like `std::string`) is designed to ensure safe and predictable behavior by properly initializing objects through their constructors. By calling the default constructor when declaring `std::string myString;`, you can be confident that `myString` is not only declared but also properly initialized and ready for use in subsequent operations.
